title: Historical and Conditional Forecasts of Sampled Net-Position Peaks
subtitle: Comparisons on an FX record and Treasury position aggregates
abstract: We evaluate established conditional methods for forecasting the maximum absolute source-reported position over the current and next H records. Historical headrooms, reanchored increment scenarios and native peaks are compared with ridge quantile regression and multivariate local quantiles. Chronological validation selects parameters from small fixed menus before the added evaluations; the previously inspected FX interval remains exploratory. On 6,625 FX origins, six-record regression with longer history lowers mean pinball loss by 12.66% relative to the original historical-headroom rule and 14.77% relative to a reference with the same completed-label pool and update schedule. Breaches nevertheless increase from 332 to 376. In a separately specified weekly Treasury-bill position aggregate, the declared six-week regression comparison raises loss by 50.79% and breaches from 28 to 54 over 277 origins. Short-history regression performs poorly at the longer horizon in both sources. A favorable secondary Treasury neighbor comparison reverses on a fixed sparse grid containing only 12 origins. A later, separately frozen exploratory AR residual replay lowers loss in five of eight cells against matched increment translation and raises it in three; breaches increase in all eight. The largest Treasury H24 gain is 24.12%, with breaches rising from 12 to 59. Observed rankings differ across the studied model-family, source, horizon and history cells. The contribution is an application and model-validation comparison using mature estimators. Aggregation, calendar horizons, estimated-forecast incoherence and downloaded vintages limit transfer. The results establish neither conditional coverage nor gains from changing quotes, hedges, capital or funding decisions.

blocks.html: A recorded net position can reach a large magnitude and return toward its starting value before a horizon ends. A forecast of the terminal signed position leaves the intervening recorded magnitudes unmeasured. We study an upper-quantile report for the largest absolute source-reported position at issue and over the next H records. It answers a passive monitoring question: does any recorded future position exceed the issued level in magnitude? The financial interpretation depends on the measurement process; a sampled netted position does not reconstruct a complete hedged book or a funding requirement.

The empirical question is whether simple historical constructions remain competitive when established conditional methods are fitted directly to this peak response. We compare historical headrooms (F), increment paths reanchored to the current signed position (S), and native historical peaks subject to the current magnitude floor (K). Earlier one-state retrieval is retained as a reference. The added procedures are ridge quantile regression (QR), multivariate nearest-neighbor quantiles (KNN), and a scale-adjusted local variant. Their 33 coordinates include position lags, current magnitude, past increment scales and recorded-clock calendar information. These are established statistical operations, not newly proposed estimators. A later closed exploratory addition compares fitted AR(1) residual-block replay with matching S/F and the previously selected QR in all eight source/horizon/history cells.

All direct training responses must have ended by the actual refit time. Historical controls with matching completed-label pools and update schedules distinguish part of the estimation-budget difference. Validation selects a small menu separately by source, horizon, history and family; all candidates and references are retained. The original FX evaluation archive had already been inspected. Publicly freezing the added procedures before their execution does not restore an unseen holdout.

The favorable FX primary and adverse Treasury primary must be read together. At H=6, QR using 2,880 completed FX episodes lowers mean loss by 12.66% against the original rolling 720-episode F rule. It also lowers loss by 14.77% against F with the same 2,880-episode frozen pool and update schedule. Breach occasions rise from 332 to 376, although mean positive overrun falls. At H=24, long-history QR improves on the old S reference by only 1.83%, with 531 rather than 287 breaches and more than doubled mean positive overrun. Short-history QR instead performs worse at that horizon.

The separate application uses an official weekly compilation of primary dealers' aggregate Treasury-bill market-value positions. It is a different financial measurement process, not a second individual FX dealer or a known-disjoint institutional panel. Its declared H=6, W=260 QR comparison has 50.79% higher loss than matched-pool F, with 54 versus 28 breaches over 277 origins. All four Treasury QR specifications lose to their own F controls. A secondary H=24 neighbor gain reverses on the fixed sparse grid. Units, histories, horizons, release conventions and revised snapshots remain source specific.

The contribution is a comparison that challenges historical peak constructions with credible conditional competitors and records the limits of transfer. The direct competitors change the original FX ranking, while the chosen QR procedure has substantial limitations on another measured position series. The later AR comparison improves on QR in all four Treasury cells and loses in three of four FX cells, requiring a family-specific interpretation. Completed-label matching does not isolate a causal information effect from regularization, function class, local response count or validation selection. Elementary geometry explains construction relationships, not predictive optimality. We claim no new calibration theorem, universal forecasting improvement or operational intervention.

sections.title: 2. Closest work and established method transfer

blocks.html: The closest empirical lineage is Wisniewski, Lindsay and Lindsay (2020), who already use nearest-neighbor and other regression engines on this FX source family, with positions over the preceding 24 hours and calendar or trading-session information. Their comparisons include quantile, conformal and normalized-conformal interval forecasts. Chapter 6 of Wisniewski's thesis continues related regularized and normalized endpoint constructions (award year 2024; inspected cover 2023). These precedents rule out first-use claims for conditional regression, lag/calendar features, neighbors or normalization on these records. Exact input-byte equality with the accepted version-2 member is not established.

Our response is a single upper quantile of an absolute multi-record maximum including the observed issue floor. A signed endpoint interval does not determine this peak: identical future-record marginals can yield different maxima when their dependence differs. The earlier paper averages two endpoint-quantile losses; its numbers cannot benchmark this single peak score. We instead refit a selected set of established engines to completed peak/headroom labels and evaluate the same response on common origins. This is not a reproduction of that earlier entire model suite.

Financial path extrema are established risk objects. MaxVaR studies the worst mark-to-market loss before a horizon under a portfolio-value first-passage framework (Boudoukh et al., 2004). Petrunia, Sabetti and Voia (2019, updated Discussion Paper 7) study the largest end-of-day net debit across ACSS participants, followed by block maxima or threshold excesses. Their cross-sectional terminal-debit maximum differs from a single series' future two-sided sampled peak. Neither precedent supports a claim that financial peak forecasting itself is new here.

Prospective payment-system liquidity forecasting also has established precedents. Arjani, Li and Sabetti (2020) predict a remaining-day payment-demand/resource ratio and its threshold exceedance using payments and credit information. That ratio is a different functional from an absolute position peak or a directional timing peak. We neither reproduce their models nor observe the settlement inputs required to validate funding adequacy. The distinction further limits broad financial-target novelty claims.

Regression-quantile loss minimization is classical (Koenker and Bassett, 1978). Biau and Patra (2011) develop sequential quantile prediction with lag-neighbor experts, growing history, truncation and loss-weighted aggregation under stated stationarity, ergodicity and regularity conditions. Our fixed pools and delayed overlapping labels do not inherit that consistency theorem. The ridge and local estimators here constitute a bounded challenge, not the strongest possible conditional-model universe. Quantile forests (Meinshausen, 2006), autoregressive quantiles such as CAViaR (Engle and Manganelli, 2004), sequential predictive conformal inference (Xu and Xie, 2023) and full volatility-updated or filtered historical simulation (Hull and White, 1998; Barone-Adesi et al., 1999) remain distinct unexecuted alternatives.

Trajectory bands and financial horizon curves also predate this comparison. Conformalized Adaptive Forecasting of Heterogeneous Trajectories (Zhou, Lindemann and Sesia, 2024, arXiv v2) uses trajectory-level calibration and a cross-trajectory exchangeability premise. Sözen (2026) combines multi-horizon expected-shortfall forecasts, shape constraints and joint calibration. Their responses and assumptions differ from this position peak; an overlapping single archive is not automatically an exchangeable set of trajectories. Chronological slicing or response normalization alone transfers no simultaneous or conditional-coverage conclusion. We report realized loss, breaches and severity without borrowing those guarantees.

The remaining distinction is the measured peak target, known floor, completed-label timing, construction/update controls and separately qualified aggregate application. A changed target or dataset alone is not a new method. The directed source search does not establish exhaustive priority for this exact target-and-data combination. Its evidence and selected reading ranges are documented separately from the experiments.

The FX input is the one-hour member of the Net Position Time Series Dataset, version 2: 18,576 records from 5 February 2014 01:00 through 24 January 2017 00:00. Wisniewski et al. (2020) describe aggregate client-flow positions across five liquid currency pairs for one market maker. We use datetime and the signed NetPosUsd scalar, rather than reconstructing raw currency positions, hedge transactions or cash movements. The source has 18,420 one-hour and 155 forty-nine-hour adjacent gaps. We preserve chronology without sorting, removing gap-crossing windows or interpolation. The timezone and historical publication/vintage convention remain unverified.

The Treasury source is the New York Fed Primary Dealer Statistics series PDPOSGS-B, identifying Treasury-bill long positions less short positions. The FR 2004 framework supplies a weekly Wednesday-close, market/fair-value basis. The accepted snapshot has 706 seven-day-spaced records from 3 April 2013 through 7 October 2026, in USD millions. It aggregates reporting dealers and can reflect valuation or reporting-composition changes. It does not identify pure customer order flow or gross exposures. Taking an absolute value after summing signed dealer positions permits cancellation; offsetting dealer positions can leave a small aggregate and large individual magnitudes (see also the aggregation discussion in Duffie et al., 2023).

Economic dates and public releases differ. New York Fed statistics normally update on Thursday for the preceding reporting week; a 2004 announcement established a one-week publication lag. Exact historical release times, holidays and original unrevised observations were not reconstructed. The inspected API routes supplied no verified historical release-vintage selector, which is not proof that no archive exists elsewhere. The Treasury exercise is a downloaded-vintage replay indexed by economic as-of date, treating the current record as known at issue by convention. It is not a live public-information or as-released backtest.

Strict loading accepts only exact source bytes, schemas, chronology and finite positions, without alias splicing. The FX CSV is 1,286,391 bytes, SHA-256 b8e92c54a76b49990b028252d6a89195e92193990e72f10228f2280a11a967fa; Treasury is 23,315 bytes, SHA-256 9f9f942ea8775a15f2e839cfe489f2e5113659ac37b375282d93bd6379be7cdb. Rolling controls take the latest W completed labels at each issue. Frozen controls use T(r,H,W), matching the conditional completed-label pool and refit schedule, while reanchoring S at current t. One-state controls select the nearest starting signed positions from the rolling eligible pool, resolving ties by recency: k=360 for FX W720, k=40 for Treasury W52 and k=80 for Treasury W260. No FX W2880 one-state reference was declared. The original construction and earlier recent/nearest menus remain historical evidence in Appendix B.

On a common set and fixed rank, let r(abs)=max|B−|N(i)|| and r(signed)=max|x−N(i)|. Elementary order-statistic and projection stability gives |F−K|≤r(abs), |S−K|≤r(signed), hence |F−S|≤r(abs)+r(signed). Appendix A proves these finite relationships and their predictive limits. Nearest signed-state membership minimizes its maximum signed distance at a given count; it need not minimize forecast loss. These statements do not automatically bound QR, scaled responses or the richer 33-coordinate distance.

The 33 raw coordinates are N(t) through N(t−24), current magnitude, short/long past increment RMS, sine/cosine of recorded hour, sine/cosine of weekday (Monday zero), and whether the just-observed adjacent gap exceeds its nominal interval. RMS spans are 24/168 FX records and 6/26 Treasury records; nominal gaps are 3600 and 604800 seconds. Calendar coordinates use the stored source clock, not a verified UTC session. Weekly calendar coordinates can be constant, and coordinates need not supply independent information.

blocks.text: 4.3. Ridge quantile and multivariate local reports

blocks.html: QR minimizes the normalized headroom regression-quantile objective with an unpenalized intercept and a ridge penalty on slopes. The fixed menu is lambda in {0.001,0.01,0.1}; tau=19/20. Training optimizes the unprojected response, while validation scores the final projected report in native units.

This real-arithmetic parameterization includes the scale factor and floor-centered penalty; the intercept remains unpenalized. The issued report is max{B,alpha+z theta}. Adding an issue-known B translates conditional quantiles of G into those of P. Raising a report below a known B≤P to B weakly reduces realized pinball loss. These elementary facts neither guarantee the fitted affine specification nor establish coverage.

For KNN, distances are squared Euclidean distances between training-standardized coordinates. Each of 25 level coordinates has weight 1/5; each coordinate of the RMS, hour and weekday pairs has weight 1/sqrt(2); magnitude and gap have weight one. Exact distance ties favor more recent training origins, and selected paired rows retain chronological order. Plain KNN reports B+Q(k selected G). Scaled KNN divides each selected historical G by its own past short RMS, stabilized below by 10<super>−6</super> a(r), and multiplies the resulting quantile by the correspondingly stabilized query RMS. The stabilizer is fixed within the refit block; no future query outcome or scale is used. This is response normalization, not a fitted dynamic path simulation.

blocks.html: The neighbor menus are {180,360,720} at both FX windows, {20,40,52} at Treasury W52, and {40,80,160} at W260. No interpolation is used; an unavailable corrected rank fails. For k=52, ceil((k+1).95)=51, while the ordinary .95 empirical pinball quantile has rank 50. Thus equal target and preference do not make all finite-sample fitting criteria identical. Plain KNN at k=W equals frozen F exactly; its distances no longer affect membership. Scaled KNN still changes responses at k=W. Long-window menus do not contain the full pool. Appendix C records numerical acceptance and failures.

After the conditional results had been inspected, we specified one additional path-propagation comparison without an order, volatility or tuning menu. At each original refit r, put a=r−H−W+1 and fit N(s)=c(r)+phi(r)N(s−1)+epsilon(s) on the unique transitions a+1,...,r. The W completed scenarios have W+H levels in their union and W+H−1 unique transitions; overlapping paths do not duplicate transitions in OLS. Coefficients and the historical pool remain fixed until the next original refit, while the query uses the actual N(t).

Using the same fitted coefficients for every residual in a block and replaying its original order from x=N(t) gives M(i,h;x)=N(i+h)+phi(r)^h[x−N(i)]. Set h0 explicitly to x and report the corrected empirical quantile of the W maximum absolute replay paths. The intercept cancels in this deterministic identity; it is still estimated in the mean recursion. At exact phi1 the arithmetic agrees with frozen S. Negative or above-one finite estimates are eligible, without clipping. Constant regressors, lost dispersion and nonfinite computations fail without a substitute model.

This is a mean-filtered ordered-block historical comparison, not the full conditional-volatility filtered simulation of Hull and White (1998) or Barone-Adesi et al. (1999). It does not standardize/rescale innovations, fit GARCH, independently draw future steps or introduce Monte Carlo randomness. Conditional representativeness of historical residual blocks remains unverified; numerical OLS acceptance supplies no coverage or mean-reversion law. Appendix A.4 gives the path relationship, and Appendix C records numerical checks.

The FX primary is H6 QR W2880 minus original rolling F W720; the Treasury primary is H6 QR W260 minus frozen F W260. These are the two declared source-specific comparisons. The FX H24 QR W2880 minus original rolling S W720 comparison is a legacy-reference sensitivity: its reference was chosen in the preceding study, not independently of all historical outcomes. No favorable secondary model replaces either primary.

The wider comparison menu places those results in context. Every selected family is compared with frozen F/S/K at its own source/H/W (72 contrasts), and rolling-minus-frozen F/S/K supplies 24 update controls. The two FX contrasts add two, totaling 98 unique comparisons; the Treasury primary is already among the 72 and is not duplicated. The later AR addition has a separate exploratory comparison set, described below, and does not change this menu.

The stipulated pinball preference weights an underprediction dollar nineteen times an overprediction dollar. It is a consistent quantile score (Gneiting, 2011), not an observed funding cost or the only possible consistent score. Paired means are aggregated from stored per-origin differences, not rounded table subtraction. Mean positive overrun averages (P−C)+ over every origin; mean unused allowance averages (C−P)+. Extra allowance C−B differs from unused allowance. Strict breaches use P>C. Conditional overrun uses each method's own breach set and denominator, with an explicit undefined reason when no event occurs.

Annual groups and the global grid t(start)+j(H+1) are descriptive sensitivities. The grid never resets by year and removes shared recorded observations between its closed label windows; shared training histories and temporal dependence remain. FX grid counts are 947/265 for H6/H24; Treasury counts are 40/12. Different source units and economic durations are not pooled. No population test, confidence interval, independent-replication count or conditional-coverage conclusion is attached to these added comparisons. The earlier original resampling profiles apply only to that historical F-minus-S sequence.

Table 2 records the complete validation-selected parameters. All 72 declared validation candidates completed. Parameter ties prefer the larger numeric candidate. Any failed or incomplete candidate makes its whole source/H/W/family cell ineligible; a failed selected evaluation has no complete loss, no shortened mean and no alternate-parameter fallback. Every actual declared phase completed.

blocks.html: The original construction study was specified at 05:46:37 UTC on 21 October 2026 and publicly committed before its target-specific forecasts/losses; it used seven settings and five methods. The subsequent one-state retrieval extension was conceived after those outcomes were inspected and retained 30 fixed configurations. Both are historical evidence, not fresh validation for the present additions. Appendix B preserves their complete loss menus and adverse outcomes.

This revision publicly froze its source, model and machine specification at commit 1bd5b692fd9cb240763c032fb4e1c203871fad55 before the first new validation phase (22 October, 09:26:23 UTC). Every selected parameter and its full validation-receipt hash was then publicly frozen at 8ce6e398a17e4c12cb36a9a76785e78fd21a1da0 before selected evaluation. The FX evaluation archive had already been inspected; this execution chronology does not restore an unseen holdout.

The root trace audit independently recomputed every source/H peak with direct maxima, checked archive hashes, origins, floors, refit indices and final scores, and reconciled all 90 method summaries, 372 annual rows and 98 paired contrasts. Twelve shared historical FX aggregate records match the earlier accepted study exactly. These checks establish execution identity and arithmetic consistency, not forecasting superiority. Numerical-vector and public-diagnostic review scopes are distinguished in Appendix C.

The later AR specification was publicly frozen at a068dfe6b4dcb2447d6d16f665fb39fe9defd329 and all seventeen bound files were freshly verified before its 11:50:31 UTC start on 22 October. It contains the eight Cartesian source/H/W cells, direct matched-S comparisons and F/selected-QR context: 24 contrasts total. Both samples were already inspected, so every new contrast is exploratory. Original primaries, selections and forecasts remain unchanged; a favorable AR cell does not replace a declared QR primary.

sections.title: 6. FX results: conditional gains depend on history and horizon

blocks.caption: Table 3. Complete conditional loss menu and same-history frozen controls on 6,625 FX origins, in USD millions. Every selected QR/KNN/scaled cell is shown. Rolling and one-state reference results and all breach/severity quantities remain in the complete CSVs.

blocks.html: The H6 primary QR W2880 loss is USD 385,844.89, against USD 441,774.04 for original rolling F W720. The direct paired mean is −USD 55,929.15, or −12.660%. Against W2880 frozen F it is −14.767%; against frozen S at that same window it is also favorable. Thus the added conditional benchmark changes the older FX ranking. The cross-window primary changes history length and update frequency as well as the estimator; the matched-pool controls address part, but not all, of this procedural difference.

The H6 gain is not uniform risk improvement. QR has 376 strict breaches (5.675%) versus 332 (5.011%) for old rolling F. Mean positive overrun falls from USD 166,531.06 to 156,123.03, while mean unused allowance falls by USD 920,830.41. More occasions breach, with a lower unconditional overrun contribution. Conditional severity uses the different method-specific event sets and cannot identify improvement on the same incidents. At W720, H6 QR improves on frozen F by only 2.117%, while scaled KNN is worse by 5.349%.

At H24, QR W2880 loss is USD 734,695.07 against USD 748,383.54 for old rolling S W720: −USD 13,688.47 (−1.829%). Breaches increase from 287 (4.332%) to 531 (8.015%); mean positive overrun rises from USD 149,813.88 to 317,678.12, while unused allowance falls. With W720, QR instead loses to frozen F by 31.504% and frozen S by 37.095%. Neither the broader model class nor a favorable short-horizon result provides a uniform advantage across history budgets.

The H6 primary loss difference is negative in both issue-year groups: −12.012% over 6,262 origins in 2016 and −29.513% over the 363-origin partial 2017. H24 improvement against its legacy reference is only −0.555% in 2016 and −33.007% in partial 2017; about 70.83% of the small total net gain comes from that short tail segment. The fixed H+1 grids retain favorable H6/H24 differences of −16.388%/−8.027%, with 947/265 origins. These subdivisions and grids are sensitivities of one inspected record, not independent replications or a basis for switching forecasts retrospectively.

sections.title: 7. Treasury results: an adverse primary transfer

blocks.caption: Table 4. Complete selected conditional loss menu and same-history frozen controls on 277 Treasury origins. Losses are in the source's USD-million units, not FX USD. H6/H24 mean six/24 weekly transitions. No monetary average is pooled across sources.

blocks.html: The declared H6 QR W260 primary has mean loss 4,159.673 versus 2,758.665 for matched frozen F, in USD millions. Its paired increase is 1,401.008 (+50.786%), with 54 rather than 28 strict breaches (19.495% versus 10.108%). Mean positive overrun rises from 1,395.639 to 3,131.862 and unused allowance falls from 28,656.166 to 23,688.088. Under the stipulated score, the reduced unused quantity does not compensate for the more heavily weighted overrun increase. This is an adverse accuracy result from numerically accepted fits, not a convergence failure.

Every Treasury QR cell loses to its own frozen F control: +83.354% and +50.786% at H6 for W52/W260, and +227.411% and +109.843% at H24. Short-history H24 QR breaches 132 of 277 responses. All four selected scaled-KNN cells also have higher loss than their matched F controls. The primary QR difference is adverse in each complete year 2021–2025. Its favorable −14.404% in 2026 covers only 16 issue origins through April, with no breaches for either method. This partial period is retained, not used to rescue the primary.

Plain KNN W52 selects k=52 at both horizons and equals frozen F at every stored issue. The distance coordinates do not change membership in these rows; they demonstrate a full-pool fallback, not rich-feature gains. At W260, selected KNN has secondary all-origin loss reductions of 3.447% (H6) and 8.964% (H24) against F. These do not replace the QR primary, and no selected conditional procedure is descriptively below every retained historical reference at its horizon. Such a whole-menu observation is not a newly selected forecast rule.

The secondary H24 KNN W260 comparison has 13 versus 12 breaches and mean overrun 327.816 versus 306.848, alongside reduced unused allowance. On the fixed 12-origin H+1 grid its mean loss is 3,111.788 against 2,807.400 for F, reversing to +10.842%. The H6 KNN sensitivity does not reverse: its 40-origin difference remains −22.071%. These exact grids remove shared recorded label observations but retain common training histories and possible time dependence. The sparse reversal does not identify a cause or prove an opposite population ranking; it does prevent a claim of stable secondary transfer.

All 24 same-source conditional cells and all 66 reference procedures completed. The complete source-specific results, all 72 common-history contrasts, 24 update controls, annual decompositions and sparse-grid contrasts remain available. The adverse Treasury primary and short-history results are not omitted or replaced by the best hindsight-selected configuration.

sections.title: 8. Exploratory dynamic replay: family-specific score and tail tradeoffs

blocks.caption: Table 5. Complete later AR comparison. Entries are within-reference mean-loss percentages; negative favors AR. S/F have matching source, H, W and refit schedule; QR is the original selected same-cell fit. Counts are AR / S strict breaches over 6,625 FX or 277 Treasury origins. Every row is exploratory; sources are not pooled.

blocks.html: AR has lower loss in five of eight cells against S, five against F and five against QR; these sets differ. Relative to QR it loses in three of four FX cells and improves in all four Treasury cells. The original adverse Treasury QR primary therefore does not establish failure of every conditional family. Against S, the FX H6 changes are −1.536%/−0.546% at W720/W2880, while H24 changes are +2.386%/+5.147%. Treasury changes are −13.444%/−18.887% at H6 and +35.125%/−24.118% at H24 for W52/W260. No additional model is selected from this table.

Against S, AR mean report and mean unused allowance decrease in every cell, while strict breach occasions increase in all eight and mean positive overrun increases in seven. Treasury H24 W260 loss falls from 2478.871 to 1881.016 USD millions (−24.118%), yet breaches rise from 12 to 59 of 277 and mean positive overrun rises from 306.848 to 892.437. Mean unused allowance falls from 43747.307 to 20664.031. Under the stipulated score, .05 times the unused reduction exceeds .95 times the added overrun. This explains the observed loss change without asserting safer limits, calibrated tails or observed financing savings.

Direct-S signs reverse for FX H24 W720 on the 265-origin grid (+2.386% overall, −1.884% sparse) and Treasury H24 W52 on only 12 origins (+35.125%, −14.100%). Treasury H24 W260 remains favorable on its sparse grid but is adverse in 2022 and 2023 (+9.928%, +20.224%). Every annual and sparse contrast remains. Observed fitted coefficients lie between zero and one, with refit means around .981–.985 for FX and .676–.850 for Treasury; these descriptions do not identify true mean reversion. Source, horizon, history and model family all matter, and neither average report reduction nor a below-one slope determines a loss ranking.

Observed rankings differ across the studied method-family, source, horizon and history cells. Long-history QR improves on the inspected FX record and loses on the separately measured Treasury aggregate. The later exploratory AR replay lowers loss in five of eight cells against matched S and raises it in three, while strict breach occasions increase in all eight. It improves on QR in all four Treasury cells and loses in three of four FX cells. The Treasury QR failure therefore remains family-specific, and average-score gains need not mean fewer tail events. None of these later results replaces either declared primary. The contribution is a bounded application/model-validation finding; elementary common-set bounds and implementation checks remain supporting evidence rather than methodological novelty.

Matching completed-label pools and update schedules improves within-source interpretability, without isolating a causal value of additional features. F/K already use current magnitude and S uses the signed current anchor; the added procedures also change function class, regularization, local count, scaling and validation selection. The two source primaries have different references, histories, refit frequencies, score units and calendar horizons, so their percentages are not estimates of one common replicated effect. No FX-fitted coefficients or transforms are moved to Treasury: each source is fitted and validated separately. Portability concerns a source-adapted procedure family.

The specification and selection budgets also limit interpretation. A post-result audit of the complete validation menu finds five of eight QR selections at penalty-menu endpoints, including all four Treasury selections. This does not show that an untested penalty would help. Treasury validation has 52 consecutive origins; at H24, at most three label windows with origins among those 52 can avoid sharing observations. This is not an effective-sample-size estimate. The complete validation-loss profiles and fixed/adapted source contract delimit the tested specifications. Selections and negative results remain unchanged; mature alternatives are not exhausted and optimality is not established.

Post-result diagnostics clarify the issued reports rather than changing their rankings. Every common realized target satisfies P(H6)≤P(H24), yet the separately fitted reports can cross: FX W720 QR crosses on 640/6,625 issues, and Treasury W52 QR on 91/277. Some short Treasury historical F/S controls also cross because the horizons use different mature episode sets; zero observed crossings supply no general guarantee. Appendix D retains all 45 original pairs and a separately frozen addition covering all four AR pairs. AR has zero observed FX crossings, but Treasury W52/W260 cross on 59/26 of 277 issues. The horizon-specific fits and mature scenario sets differ; numerical acceptance does not establish an ordered report curve.

The floor diagnostic distinguishes a binding issued report from an outcome atom. Treasury H24 QR W52 has breaches both at and away from its floor, so poor accuracy cannot be attributed solely to floor binding; Appendix D retains the full event counts. Stored equality cannot distinguish unprojected negative, exactly zero and rounded headrooms. Projection onto the known floor weakly improves realized pinball loss, but a learned H6 report is not a known lower bound for the H24 outcome: forcing H24 above H6 has no analogous automatic improvement argument. No forecast reconciliation or post-result retuning is performed.

A near-five-percent empirical breach rate does not certify a conditional 95% envelope. The response can have an atom at its current magnitude, so even a true quantile need not have exactly five-percent strict exceedance. Refitted histories, selected neighborhoods, overlapping labels and finite validation remain dependent. We have not established the assumptions needed for the published asymptotic or conformal results discussed in Section 2. Numerical convergence and arithmetic reproducibility do not remove those statistical limitations.

A separately frozen late fixed-terminal diagnostic examines the stronger datewise conditional strict-breach upper-bound null. Four of 56 matched reports cross the declared formal reference threshold, all specific QR configurations; the other 52 do not receive a coverage PASS. Appendix D retains every report and phase and distinguishes fixed-procedure theory from the inspected-sample selection history. Treasury H24 W260 AR still has 59 breaches in 277 issues despite not crossing that threshold. This addition changes neither the score comparisons nor the missing independent validation.

The Treasury application broadens the observed measurement process while leaving compatible individual-dealer validation and original-release forecasting unresolved. Cross-dealer cancellation, market-value accounting, reporting composition, weekly sampling and the downloaded economic-date convention limit its financial interpretation. These qualifications apply to favorable and adverse outcomes; they do not justify dismissing the adverse primary after observation. A perfectly offset aggregate can be zero while individual dealer magnitudes are arbitrarily large, and sampled observations impose no finite bound on inter-record excursions without additional path restrictions. Further compatible records and an original-release replay remain open research questions, not completed evidence.

Operational claims require data on quotes, fills, hedges, book decomposition, cash flows, collateral and financing prices, none of which is observed here. Active inventory-sensitive quoting models, such as Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008), concern decisions that can change the position process; these interventions are not evaluated here. A netted position envelope is therefore not optimal capital, cash adequacy, a funding saving, profit or a recommendation to change risk limits. Mean loss, report levels, breach frequency and severity describe passive reports under stipulated weights.

Established conditional methods materially change an earlier sampled-peak comparison; observed rankings differ across the studied model-family, source, horizon and history cells. The FX six-record QR primary lowers loss by 12.66% with more breach occasions; its matched-pool improvement is 14.77%. The separately specified Treasury six-week QR primary raises loss by 50.79% and increases breaches. Short-history regressions, a secondary neighbor sensitivity reversal and post-result horizon incoherence limit a general success narrative. The later exploratory AR replay improves on QR in all four Treasury cells and loses in three of four FX cells. Against matched S it lowers loss in five cells and raises it in three, while breaches increase in all eight. Its long-history Treasury H24 gain accompanies 59 rather than 12 breaches. Complete adverse and favorable comparisons are retained; this supplement does not replace either original primary. The evidence supports a bounded comparison of mature forecasting procedures on two measured financial position series, not a new estimator, conditional-coverage theorem or operational risk-policy gain.

sections.title: Appendix A. Finite geometry and its predictive limits

blocks.html: These construction arguments concern F/S/K on an identical historical set and rank. They are retained from the earlier comparison. A one-dimensional signed-distance minimax property does not extend automatically to the multivariate neighbor distance, and the bounds do not automatically constrain QR or scale-adjusted responses.

These are elementary finite-array arguments, rather than new asymptotic or coverage results. Fix a nonempty common selected set J, an available rank 1≤k≤|J|, query x=N<sub>t</sub>, floor B=|x| and completed historical windows. All identities in this appendix concern real arithmetic. Write B<sub>i</sub>=|N<sub>i</sub>|, d<sub>i,h</sub>=N<sub>i+h</sub>−N<sub>i</sub>, with d<sub>i,0</sub>=0, and define

Let a(i)=min over h of d(i,h) and b(i)=max over h of d(i,h), so a(i)≤0≤b(i). These are the lower and upper increments denoted l and u in Section 4. The auxiliary nonnegative envelope coordinates below use u(i)=b(i) and v(i)=−a(i).
A<sub>i</sub>=B+P<sub>i</sub>−B<sub>i</sub>;   T<sub>i</sub>=max<sub>0≤h≤H</sub>|x+d<sub>i,h</sub>|;   C<sub>B</sub>(z)=max(B,z).

Both A<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>i</sub> are at least B. The projection C<sub>B</sub> is nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz. It commutes with a finite order statistic, as does a common translation. Hence F<sub>J</sub>=Q<sub>k</sub>(A), S<sub>J</sub>=Q<sub>k</sub>(T) and K<sub>J</sub>=Q<sub>k</sub>(C<sub>B</sub>(P)). Since C<sub>B</sub>(A<sub>i</sub>)=A<sub>i</sub>,
|A<sub>i</sub>−C<sub>B</sub>(P<sub>i</sub>)|≤|A<sub>i</sub>−P<sub>i</sub>|=|B−B<sub>i</sub>|.

The reverse triangle inequality bounds each path value's change under a starting-position translation by |x−N<sub>i</sub>|. Taking a maximum gives |T<sub>i</sub>−P<sub>i</sub>|≤|x−N<sub>i</sub>|. Applying the same floor projection preserves that bound because T<sub>i</sub>≥B. Finally, paired order statistics are nonexpansive in the maximum coordinate difference: if |u<sub>i</sub>−v<sub>i</sub>|≤r for every i, then u<sub>i</sub>≤v<sub>i</sub>+r and conversely; monotonicity and common translation give |Q<sub>k</sub>(u)−Q<sub>k</sub>(v)|≤r. These observations prove the two K bounds in Section 4. The triangle inequality and ||N<sub>i</sub>|−|x||≤|N<sub>i</sub>−x| prove the stated F/S bound. Keeping the rank fixed while changing one side's historical rows does not by itself justify these common-set comparison bounds.

Among all size-m subsets, selecting the m smallest signed distances minimizes the largest selected distance: any alternative must include an element at least as far away as the mth ordered distance. This finite minimax fact, with the declared tie convention, concerns the signed radius. It does not minimize the absolute-anchor radius, the sum of the two radii, the actual report gap or a forecast loss. For every fixed realized y, pinball loss is max(τ,1−τ)-Lipschitz in its report, so a report-gap bound also bounds the absolute loss difference. Such stability supplies no sign for the realized or expected loss difference.

blocks.text: A.2. Envelope plateaus and the role of signed anchors

blocks.html: Put u<sub>i</sub>=b<sub>i</sub>≥0 and v<sub>i</sub>=−a<sub>i</sub>≥0. The headroom of an increment envelope at any anchor z is
g<sub>i</sub>(z)=max(z+u<sub>i</sub>,−z+v<sub>i</sub>)−|z|; for z≥0 it equals max(u<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>i</sub>−2z), and for z≤0 it equals max(u<sub>i</sub>+2z,v<sub>i</sub>).

F pools each envelope's headroom at its historical anchor, g<sub>i</sub>(N<sub>i</sub>); S pools its headroom at the query, g<sub>i</sub>(x). The branches agree at zero and together make g<sub>i</sub> 2-Lipschitz, with range lying in [min(u<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>i</sub>),max(u<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>i</sub>)]. Apply the distance and range bounds to each paired row, then use the same-rank order-statistic stability from A.1 to obtain
|F<sub>J</sub>−S<sub>J</sub>|≤max<sub>i in J</sub>min{2|x−N<sub>i</sub>|,|u<sub>i</sub>−v<sub>i</sub>|}.

For example, u<sub>i</sub>=v<sub>i</sub> in every row makes F<sub>J</sub>=S<sub>J</sub> at arbitrary anchors. Nonnegative query/source anchors together with u<sub>i</sub>≥v<sub>i</sub> in every row also suffice; the nonpositive analogue uses v<sub>i</sub>≥u<sub>i</sub>. These are sufficient conditions, not a characterization: pooled order statistics can coincide even when paired rows differ. The range bound also gives F<sub>J</sub>,S<sub>J</sub>≤R<sub>J</sub>, where R<sub>J</sub>=B+Q<sub>k</sub>{max(u<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>i</sub>):i in J}. This is a theoretical same-set ordering; no R retrieval configuration is evaluated in the extension, and the ordering does not make R<sub>J</sub> preferable under a given loss.

If every B<sub>i</sub>≤B, then A<sub>i</sub>≥C<sub>B</sub>(P<sub>i</sub>) and F<sub>J</sub>≥K<sub>J</sub>. If every B<sub>i</sub>≥B, then C<sub>B</sub>(P<sub>i</sub>)=P<sub>i</sub>≥A<sub>i</sub> and F<sub>J</sub>≤K<sub>J</sub>. Equal absolute anchors force F=K but leave signs relevant to S. A coherent full-pool example uses c>0, H=1, n=720, τ=19/20, t=721 and N<sub>s</sub>=(−1)<super>s+1</super>c for 0≤s≤721. The pool uses completed labels at origins J={1,...,720}, with 360 anchors of each sign and current N<sub>t</sub>=c. All native peaks equal c and headrooms equal zero, so F=K=c. Raw reanchoring gives 360 peaks c and 360 peaks 3c; rank 685 gives S=3c. Thus r<sub>abs</sub>=0 while r<sub>signed</sub>=2c and |S−K|=2c. This artificial path respects maturity and an available corrected rank; it is not an empirical claim or a claim about which rows nearest retrieval selects.

blocks.text: A.3. The same observed history allows opposite loss rankings

blocks.html: Choose d>0, H≥1, 0<τ<1 and n large enough that k=ceil((n+1)τ)≤n. Set t=H+n−1 and N<sub>s</sub>=d(t−s) for 0≤s≤t, using J={0,...,n−1}. Every selected response ends by t. Each historical peak is its own positive starting value, so G<sub>i</sub>=0 and F=0. Each increment path equals −dh; reanchoring at N<sub>t</sub>=0 gives S=Hd. Two continuations of this identical observed history yield:

blocks.caption: Table A1. Artificial coherent continuations. Symbols are constructed quantities, not source-record estimates.

blocks.html: Either report can therefore have strictly smaller realized loss under a compatible future. A report ordering also need not hold universally. Consider the artificial history (0,−4,−1,2), with H=1, n=3, τ=3/4, issue t=3 and J={0,1,2}. The current anchor and floor are x=B=2; all three historical windows are completed. Table A2 shows the native and raw-reanchored paths.

blocks.caption: Table A2. Completed H=1 windows from one artificial history, in arbitrary position units. P is the native peak, G the native headroom and T the peak after reanchoring at x=2. These values are not source-record estimates.

blocks.html: The available corrected rank is ceil((3+1)3/4)=3. The third order statistics of G, T−B and P are 4, 3 and 4, respectively, so F=6, S=5 and K=4. The small pool and τ=3/4 belong only to this illustration. It contains no observation after issue and gives no realized query loss. These constructions establish logical limits, not the conditional law of the recorded series or a population ranking. A deterministic construction can refute an unconditional mathematical assertion while supplying no empirical validation for either rule.

blocks.text: A.4. Raw translation versus fixed-coefficient residual replay

blocks.html: For interpretation, fix common coefficients c and phi in N(s+1)=c+phi N(s)+epsilon(s). Replay a historical window's ordered innovations from query x. The coefficients may be treated as fixed after a refit; this algebra does not assert that they are the true dynamics. Denote replay by M and raw translation by W. Subtracting the two recursions and using induction gives
M<sub>i,h</sub>(x)=N<sub>i+h</sub>+φ<super>h</super>(x−N<sub>i</sub>);   W<sub>i,h</sub>(x)=N<sub>i+h</sub>+(x−N<sub>i</sub>).
Taking the maximum absolute path value yields
|max<sub>h</sub>|W<sub>i,h</sub>(x)|−max<sub>h</sub>|M<sub>i,h</sub>(x)||≤max<sub>0≤h≤H</sub>|1−φ<super>h</super>| |x−N<sub>i</sub>|.

For 0≤φ≤1 the coefficient is 1−φ<super>H</super>; at φ=1 the paths coincide. The identity needs no innovation law, while treating past innovations as representative of future conditional innovations is a separate assumption. Section 8 fits a specified mean recursion and compares realized loss, but does not validate that conditional innovation assumption. The extrema suffice to evaluate the peak after raw translation, but generally not after the dynamic correction, which depends on path order. The same-rank reports inherit a deterministic bound with max over historical anchor distances, not a guaranteed sign of loss improvement. Conditional validity remains a separate question.

sections.title: Appendix C. Numerical, rank and reproduction conventions

blocks.html: All issued reports use stored float64 values. Historical ranks retain repeated responses without interpolation. An unavailable rank stops. The corrected ranks for k=20,40,52,80,160,180,360,720 are 20,39,51,77,153,172,343,685. A corrected rank is not always an empirical pinball minimizer: k=52 selects rank51 instead of the ordinary .95 rank50. At integral k tau, the upper adjacent order statistic is an endpoint of the real-arithmetic empirical minimizer interval. Neither fact establishes future coverage.

For S, the translated peak is computed first, current B is subtracted before ranking, then B is added. Final losses use direct stored error P−C, not an algebraically equivalent differently rounded headroom residual. The fitter evaluates its complementary weight as 1−tau; final scoring converts 19/20 and 1/20 separately to floats. Display rounding never defines a breach, tie or model selection. Null conditional severities and relative differences retain explicit denominator reasons.

QR implements mature two-block convex ADMM (Boyd et al., 2011), with 34 coefficients, an unpenalized intercept, penalty rho=1/W, at most 10000 iterations, absolute tolerance 10<super>−6</super> and relative tolerance 10<super>−5</super>. Training checks finite values and linear-system solve residuals. Acceptance requires both primal and dual ADMM residual thresholds and a separate feasible-dual objective-gap condition. These numerical checks do not certify a statistical forecasting law.
P<sub>lambda</sub>=mean ρ<sub>τ</sub>(y−Xb)+(λ/2)||β||<super>2</super>;   D<sub>lambda</sub>(ν)=mean(νy)−||Z<super>T</super>ν/W||<super>2</super>/(2λ).

Here y=G/a, X includes an intercept and Z its standardized slopes. The candidate dual vector satisfies tau−1≤nu≤tau and exact zero sum on an inward 2<super>−40</super> dyadic grid; integer box limits use the exact binary-float representation of tau. The checksum checks the represented vector exactly, while objectives remain floating-point evaluations. A nonnegative Fenchel/stationarity decomposition evaluates the gap without subtracting similar objectives; the objective difference must agree within 256 machine epsilons times max(1,|P|,|D|), and the stable gap must be at most 10<super>−6</super>(1+|P|). This is not interval-arithmetic certification.

All 72 validation candidates and 24 selected evaluations passed their declared numerical/resource conditions; 768 validation and 1196 evaluation QR refits were accepted. Other conditional families have the same respective refit-event counts, not independent replications. Public receipts retain scalar diagnostics and coefficient/dual-vector hashes. Public-only review checked their acceptance and maturity metadata; it did not reconstruct hidden coefficient vectors. Separate root checks used private forecast arrays and direct source-window maxima to reconcile realized outcomes and scores. Analytic and independently enumerated small convex fixtures, causal future perturbations and explicit failures support the implementation checks.

One requested numerical thread and one financial worker ran at a time. Each phase had internal 540-second/1.5-GiB stops and a 600-second alarm. Measured validation-worker peak RSS was at most 69,746,688 bytes; evaluation/reference peak was 67,584,000 bytes, maximum phase time 15.827 seconds, and maximum observed worker threads one at recorded snapshots. Total reported worker compute was about 45.125 seconds for validation and 73.838 seconds for evaluation/references. Audit processes are measured separately. These are recorded process high-water/snapshot measurements, not a continuous thread bound, an OS hard-memory sandbox or research hours.

The public result package contains all 56 phase receipts, 72 candidate summaries, 90 evaluated procedure summaries, 372 annual rows, 98 paired means, 388 annual paired rows and 98 sparse paired rows. The first aggregate audit was tightened for finite/nonnegative numerical metadata, parameter-label binding, terminal fields and parsing the exact hashed archive bytes. Its second pass reproduced all 38 existing table/receipt export bytes unchanged; no forecasts or frozen scientific files changed. Original audit versions are retained.

Exact numerical reproduction requires the pinned source snapshots and frozen code/specification, not merely a current download or the same series label. Source routes may change their bytes through revision or expansion. New phase receipts have new timestamps/resources and therefore different hashes even if numerical forecasts agree; they must not overwrite archived evidence. The shared structured paper content generates TeX and the separately rendered supplied PDF; document generation reads approved text and aggregate-only figures, not raw financial inputs.

The public route separates archive verification from recomputation. With the pinned inputs, reproduce_conditional.py replicate creates a new attempt and serially reruns all 56 phases; its archive-only mode reads no raw source. The recorded replay matched all 24 selections, all 72 validation candidate scalar rows and all six aggregate CSV bytes. It took 129.50 seconds, with maximum worker RSS 68,911,104 bytes and one observed worker thread. The separate diagnostic replay reproduced all 90 floor and 45 horizon rows byte-for-byte without another model fit. Commands, genuine new receipt identities and measurements are in the repository guide. This computation reproduction uses the same source versions and supplies no new validation sample.

The separate AR implementation uses a finite common power-of-two scale and anchor-centered OLS cross-products, followed by numerical normal-equation checks. An independent large-offset artificial-input challenge exposed a defect in an earlier unexecuted implementation; it was repaired before the new freeze. All 399 combined synthetic tests then passed. The financial addition completed all eight cells in 10.692 seconds at its final checkpoint, with peak process RSS 104,251,392 bytes and one observed OS thread. A separate scalar/Fraction readback reconciled all 192 aggregate rows, 24 selected exact OLS fits and 24 scalar recursive reports; it checks arithmetic, not financial model adequacy.

sections.title: Appendix D. Explicitly post-result report diagnostics

blocks.html: After viewing and publishing the complete primary results, we recorded a descriptive floor-binding/horizon-coherence plan and evaluated the already accepted forecasts. These checks are not part of the 98 before-execution contrast menu, and they modify no forecast or tuning choice. The original 90 configurations and 45 source/window/method pairs are retained in post-result-floor.csv and post-result-horizon.csv, with hashes and process resources in their separate audit. Every common realized target satisfies P(H6)≤P(H24). Those files cover the original QR/KNN/scaled-KNN study and its historical controls. The later AR diagnostics are separate files; the original tables and forecasts are unchanged.

blocks.caption: Table D1. Original QR/KNN/scaled-KNN horizon-coherence diagnostics; the later AR addition is not included. A crossing means stored C(H6)>C(H24), with no tolerance used to redefine the event. Maximum gap is displayed in USD millions (FX divided by 10^6; Treasury already in that unit). The distinct financial quantities are not pooled.

blocks.html: Historical short Treasury controls also cross: rolling F/S on 38/37 issues, frozen F/S on 39/39, and one-state F/S/K on 20/20/3. Treasury W260 one-state K crosses on 13; its other historical controls and all listed FX historical controls have zero recorded crossings. Their H-specific mature sets differ, so common-set construction monotonicity is no guarantee across these procedures. The two selected k=W52 KNN reports equal their F counterparts, including the 39 crossings.

Exact floor equality describes a stored report, not an observed negative latent prediction. Treasury H24 QR W52 binds on 65 issues (58 breaches), with another 74 breaches off the floor; W260 binds on three (two breaches), with 82 others. The realized zero-headroom outcomes are 14/277 at H24 and 50/277 at H6. FX has 662/6,625 and 1,523/6,625 respectively. These descriptive event sets do not identify the cause of misspecification or effective independent sample size.

The separate AR addition retains all eight floor configurations and four same-source/window horizon pairs. FX W720/W2880 have no observed crossings over 6,625 origins each; Treasury W52/W260 have 59/26 over 277 (21.300%/9.386%), with maximum positive gaps 11784.473/5347.870 USD millions. Every realized target is ordered. Treasury W52 AR binds its floor on seven issues at each horizon, with five H6 and seven H24 breaches. The other six AR configurations never bind. Those empty-group breach rates are undefined, not zero. These inspected-sample diagnostics establish neither a cause nor a coverage guarantee.

The report-order problem does not by itself justify a particular repair. For example, B=0, P(H6)=P(H24)=1, C(H6)=10 and C(H24)=1 satisfy the target order. Raising the long report to the short one changes its .95 loss from zero to .45. This artificial real-arithmetic example is not source data; it distinguishes a learned report from a known lower bound. No isotonic reconciliation, horizon switching or post-result parameter search was run.

The original AR diagnostic command remains restricted to its retained manifest-bound attempt. A separate demonstrated fresh-attempt route now chains run_ar1_replay.py, verify_ar1_output.py and reproduce_ar1_diagnostics.py, with new identifiers and the actual hash of a genuinely generated version-2 readback. Its public guide is results/revision-20261022/ar1-fresh-reproduction/README.md. The new eight-cell AR execution reproduced all six aggregate CSVs (192 rows) and both eight/four-row diagnostic tables byte-for-byte, retaining the adverse counts without rerunning the 56 conditional phases. AR took 8.85 seconds externally with 102,629,376 bytes peak RSS and one observed OS thread. Separate arithmetic checks cover 24 exact represented-input OLS fits, 24 scalar-recursion reports and all 236 diagnostic fields; they do not independently recompute every fit. New private vectors are generated locally. This reproduction establishes neither independent data validation nor model adequacy.

A later exploratory diagnostic uses the bounded strict hit I=1{P>C}, with equality a nonbreach, and the null that its conditional expectation given full issue information is at most alpha=1/20 at every declared issue. It is not unconditional equal-loss testing or exact exceedance identification at a floor atom. Conditional-moment betting and delayed binary evidence are mature precedents (Casgrain et al., 2023, v2; Henzi and Ziegel, 2022, v3). For a fixed alternative u in [alpha,1], the hit/no-hit factor is u/alpha or (1−u)/(1−alpha); its null conditional expectation is at most one. Every globally anchored H+1 phase retains only issues whose previous same-phase target has resolved.
E<sub>n,k</sub> = [1/(1−α)] ∫<sub>α</sub><super>1</super> (u/α)<super>k</super> [(1−u)/(1−α)]<super>n−k</super> du.
E<sub>cell</sub> = [1/(H+1)] ∑<sub>r=0</sub><super>H</super> E<sub>n(r),k(r)</sub>; α=1/20.

The prior mixes each whole phase product, then all phases receive equal weight; empty phases have value one. Iterated expectation and nonnegative averaging justify a fixed-terminal e-value for a genuinely fixed causal procedure under the stated null, without independence, stationarity or a financial-magnitude moment assumption. This gives no full-filtration supermartingale or arbitrary-stopping claim. The complete matched family has 56 labels, including aliases, and excludes 24 rolling and 18 one-state reports. Its formal reference threshold is 56/(1/20)=1120. Because this diagnostic and family were chosen after inspecting results, the crossings do not obtain retrospective empirical five-percent familywise error control. The fixed-procedure proof also does not establish individually calibrated e-values or p-values for this same-sample, post-selected analysis: selection need not be measurable at the original issue times. No prior, phase or menu was retuned.

blocks.caption: Table D2. All 56 late fixed-terminal evidence diagnostics, rounded to three significant figures; * marks an exact crossing of the fixed 1120 reference threshold. TB is the separately fitted Treasury aggregate; F/S/K are the matched frozen controls. A noncrossing is not coverage certification, and evidence magnitude is not a financial-quality ranking. All 896 phase rows and exact rational identities are retained in the supplement.

blocks.html: The four reference crossings are FX H24 W720 QR and Treasury H6 W52/W260 and H24 W52 QR. Treasury H24 W260 AR has 59/277 strict hits and evidence 11.0284, below 1120; this does not negate its adverse breach record. Two Treasury QR cells both have 84/277 hits but very different evidence: about 1.311×10<super>8</super> at H6 W52 and 59.4235 at H24 W260. Their phase sizes and hit allocation differ, as do their forecasting tasks. No power calculation, equivalence or sharpness conclusion follows. Production retained all 56 summary and 896 phase rows; a distinct integer-formula readback recomputed every hit, phase and exact value. The two processes took 1.19 and 1.18 seconds externally, with peak RSS of 92,766,208 and 79,855,616 bytes and one observed thread each. No raw source, model refit or report repair was used. Complete inputs, proof, commands and measurement scope are in results/revision-20261022/coverage-evalues/README.md.

Figure 2. The two declared source primaries and FX H24 legacy-reference sensitivity: relative mean-loss, overrun and unused-allowance changes, plus breach-rate differences in percentage points. These are separate descriptive quantities, not a combined utility or monetary saving. A reduced unused quantity is not automatically overall improvement.
